\label{lemma-fibred-gives-fibred-groupoids}
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a category.
Let $p : \mathcal{S} \to \mathcal{C}$ be a fibred category.
Let $\mathcal{S}'$ be the subcategory of $\mathcal{S}$ defined
as follows
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\Ob(\mathcal{S}') = \Ob(\mathcal{S})$, and
\item for $x, y \in \Ob(\mathcal{S}')$ the set of morphisms between $x$
and $y$ in $\mathcal{S}'$ is the set of strongly cartesian morphisms between
$x$ and $y$ in $\mathcal{S}$.
\end{enumerate}
Let $p' : \mathcal{S}' \to \mathcal{C}$ be the restriction of $p$
to $\mathcal{S}'$. Then $p' : \mathcal{S}' \to \mathcal{C}$ is fibred
in groupoids.

original_source_statement_tex:
\label{lemma-2-product-fibred-categories}
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a category.
The $2$-category of categories fibred in groupoids
over $\mathcal{C}$ has 2-fibre products, and they are described as in
Lemma \ref{lemma-2-product-categories-over-C}.
statement: Let $\mathcal C$ be a category and let $F:\mathcal X\to\mathcal S$ and $G:\mathcal Y\to\mathcal S$ be morphisms of categories fibred in groupoids over $\mathcal C$. Their $2$-fibre product exists in the $2$-category of categories fibred in groupoids over $\mathcal C$. Explicitly, its objects are quadruples $(U,x,y,\alpha)$ with $U\in\Ob(\mathcal C)$, $x\in\mathcal X_U$, $y\in\mathcal Y_U$, and $\alpha:F(x)\xrightarrow{\sim}G(y)$ in $\mathcal S_U$. Its morphisms are pairs $(a,b)$ over the same base arrow $U\to U'$ satisfying $G(b)\circ\alpha=\alpha'\circ F(a)$. This again defines a category fibred in groupoids over $\mathcal C$ and, with its projections, has the stated universal property.
hypotheses: Let $\mathcal C$ be a category, and let $\mathcal X\to\mathcal S\leftarrow\mathcal Y$ be a span of categories fibred in groupoids over $\mathcal C$.
conclusions: Their $2$-fibre product exists in the $2$-category of categories fibred in groupoids over $\mathcal C$. Explicitly, its objects are quadruples $(U,x,y,\alpha)$ with $U\in\Ob(\mathcal C)$, $x\in\mathcal X_U$, $y\in\mathcal Y_U$, and $\alpha:F(x)\xrightarrow{\sim}G(y)$ in $\mathcal S_U$. Its morphisms are pairs $(a,b)$ over the same base arrow $U\to U'$ satisfying $G(b)\circ\alpha=\alpha'\circ F(a)$. This again defines a category fibred in groupoids over $\mathcal C$ and, with its projections, has the stated universal property.
semantic_review_note: Pinned 2-fibre-product lemma at lines 7228–7234 says the 2-category of categories fibred in groupoids over C admits 2-fibre products, with the construction referenced from the earlier categories-over-C lemma. The standalone expansion into quadruples (U,x,y,α) with α an ISOMORPHISM in the common fibre, compatible base-arrow morphisms, and the bicategorical universal property retains the essential 2-fibre-product structure and groupoid-fibred conclusion.

original_source_statement_tex:
\label{lemma-equivalence-fibred-categories}
Let $p : \mathcal{S}\to \mathcal{C}$ and
$p' : \mathcal{S'}\to \mathcal{C}$ be categories fibred in groupoids, and
suppose that $G : \mathcal{S}\to \mathcal {S}'$ is a functor over
$\mathcal{C}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Then $G$ is faithful (resp.\ fully faithful, resp.\ an equivalence)
if and only if for each $U\in\Ob(\mathcal{C})$ the induced functor
$G_U : \mathcal{S}_U\to \mathcal{S}'_U$ is faithful
(resp.\ fully faithful, resp.\ an equivalence).
\item If $G$ is an equivalence, then $G$ is an equivalence in the
$2$-category of categories fibred in groupoids over $\mathcal{C}$.
\end{enumerate}

\label{lemma-fully-faithful-diagonal-equivalence}
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a category. Let $p : \mathcal{S}\to \mathcal{C}$ and
$p' : \mathcal{S'}\to \mathcal{C}$ be categories fibred in groupoids.
Let $G : \mathcal{S}\to \mathcal {S}'$ be a functor over $\mathcal{C}$.
Then $G$ is fully faithful if and only if the diagonal
$$
\Delta_G :
\mathcal{S}
\longrightarrow
\mathcal{S} \times_{G, \mathcal{S}', G} \mathcal{S}
$$
is an equivalence.

Let $p : \mathcal{S} \to \mathcal{C}$ be a category fibred in groupoids.
Let $x \to y$ and $z \to y$ be morphisms of $\mathcal{S}$.
If $p(x) \times_{p(y)} p(z)$ exists, then
$x \times_y z$ exists and $p(x \times_y z) = p(x) \times_{p(y)} p(z)$.
